prompt: *(Practice question)* What is the value of $2 + 0 + 2 + 1$?

solutions.title: Ignore the zero
solutions.body:
Adding 0 changes nothing, so it is $2 + 2 + 1 = 5$.

**Answer: (E) 5**

prompt: *(Practice question)* Which of these shapes is **not** a rectangle?

solutions.title: Look for straight sides
solutions.body:
A rectangle has four straight sides and four right angles. Shapes A, B, D and E are rectangles (some are turned or long and thin). Shape C is an oval (ellipse) with no straight sides.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Turning does not matter
solutions.body:
Turning a rectangle round does not stop it being a rectangle, so B and D still count. The only shape with curved edges is C.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt:
I buy 10 plastic dinosaurs at 99p each and give the shopkeeper a £10 note.

How much change should I receive?

solutions.title: Work out the cost
solutions.body:
$10 \times 99\text{p} = 990\text{p} = £9.90$. Change from £10: $£10 - £9.90 = 10\text{p}$.

**Answer: (B) 10p**

solutions.title: Change per dinosaur
solutions.body:
Each dinosaur costs 1p less than £1. Ten of them cost 10p less than £10, so the change is 10p.

**Answer: (B) 10p**

prompt: Which of the following is closest to the length of a car?

solutions.title: Compare with things you know
solutions.body:
A car is about as long as two adults lying head to toe, roughly 4 metres. 40 cm is a toy car; 40 m is longer than a tennis court.

**Answer: (C) 4 m**

solutions.title: Use a parking space
solutions.body:
A parking space is about 5 m long and a car fits in it with a little room left over, so about 4 m.

**Answer: (C) 4 m**

prompt:
An elephant's height is about twice the circumference of one of its feet.

The circumference of one of Nellie's feet is 150 cm.

About how tall is she?

solutions.title: Double it
solutions.body:
Twice 150 cm is 300 cm, which is 3 m.

**Answer: (C) 3 m**

solutions.title: Convert first
solutions.body:
150 cm is 1.5 m, and $2 \times 1.5 = 3$ m.

**Answer: (C) 3 m**

prompt:
Emma decided to paint on her bedroom wall the 11 letters of the word

**MATHEMATICS**

During a school holiday, she painted one letter each day.

She finished on a Friday.

On which day of the week did she paint the first letter?

solutions.title: Count back
solutions.body:
The 11th letter was painted on Friday, so the 1st letter was 10 days earlier. 7 days before Friday is a Friday; 3 more days back is Tuesday.

**Answer: (B) Tuesday**

solutions.title: Count forwards from each option
solutions.body:
Starting on Tuesday: Tue (M), Wed (A), Thu (T), Fri (H), Sat (E), Sun (M), Mon (A), Tue (T), Wed (I), Thu (C), Fri (S) ✓.

**Answer: (B) Tuesday**

prompt:
The pie chart on the right shows the numbers of pupils who answered the question "Is there life in Outer Space?" with a "yes" or "no".

There were 21 pupils who answered "yes".

How many pupils answered "no"?

solutions.title: Read the fractions
solutions.body:
The "no" part is a right angle, a quarter of the circle, so "yes" is three quarters. Three quarters is 21 pupils, so one quarter is $21 \div 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

solutions.title: Compare the parts
solutions.body:
The "yes" part is 3 times as big as the "no" part, so "no" $= 21 \div 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

prompt:
On the first day of this month, the sun rose at Greenwich at 06:54 and set 9 hours and 40 minutes later.

At what time did the sun set?

solutions.title: Add 10 hours, take 20 minutes
solutions.body:
9 hours 40 minutes is 20 minutes less than 10 hours. $06{:}54 + 10$ hours $= 16{:}54$, minus 20 minutes $= 16{:}34$.

**Answer: (C) 16:34**

solutions.title: Add in steps
solutions.body:
$06{:}54 + 9$ hours $= 15{:}54$. Then 6 minutes takes it to 16:00 and 34 more minutes to 16:34 ($6 + 34 = 40$).

**Answer: (C) 16:34**

prompt:
Hannah places a mirror after the word SWIMS like this (see the picture).

What would the reflection look like in the mirror?

solutions.title: Reverse and flip
solutions.body:
In a mirror the word appears in reverse order, S M I W S, and each letter is flipped left-to-right. M, I and W look the same when flipped, but each S becomes a back-to-front S. Option D shows exactly this (and has W and M the right way round).

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Check letter by letter
solutions.body:
The letter nearest the mirror (the last S) appears nearest the mirror in the reflection, so the reflection starts with a back-to-front S, then M, I, W, and ends with a back-to-front S. Options C and E have normal S's, and A and B have the letters in the wrong order.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt:
The shape on the right (shown first in the picture) is rotated 90° clockwise about the point $P$.

Which of the following shows the shape as it now looks?

solutions.title: Follow the triangle
solutions.body:
Before turning, the triangle on top of the white square points up. A quarter turn clockwise makes it point to the right. That rules out A, C and D. The dark square, which was on the upper right of the triangle, turns to end up below the triangle, which is option B.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Turn the paper
solutions.body:
Draw the shape, put your pencil point on $P$ and turn the paper a quarter turn clockwise (like a clock hand going from 12 to 3). The white square stays next to $P$, the triangle now points right and the dark square is underneath it — option B.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt:
Farmer Baar has 36 sheep, some pink and the rest white.

There are twice as many pink sheep as white sheep.

How many of the sheep are pink?

solutions.title: Share into parts
solutions.body:
For every 1 white sheep there are 2 pink ones: 3 parts. One part is $36 \div 3 = 12$, so there are $2 \times 12 = 24$ pink sheep.

**Answer: (D) 24**

solutions.title: Check the options
solutions.body:
If 24 are pink, then 12 are white, and 24 is twice 12 ✓.

**Answer: (D) 24**

prompt:
Sir Pent has a tank with 4 snakes in it.

Slither is twice as long as Monty.

Viper is half as long as Slither.

Rattle is 15 cm long, and half the length of Viper.

How long is Monty?

solutions.title: Work through the snakes
solutions.body:
Rattle is 15 cm and half of Viper, so Viper is 30 cm. Viper is half of Slither, so Slither is 60 cm. Slither is twice Monty, so Monty is 30 cm.

**Answer: (B) 30 cm**

solutions.title: Spot the shortcut
solutions.body:
Slither is twice Monty and also twice Viper, so Monty and Viper are the same length: $2 \times 15 = 30$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 30 cm**

prompt:
Jonathan the tortoise eats 20 g of salad leaves a day.

The leaves are sold in 80 g bags which cost 90p.

How much would it cost to feed Jonathan for 4 weeks?

solutions.title: Days per bag
solutions.body:
One bag lasts $80 \div 20 = 4$ days. Four weeks is 28 days, which needs $28 \div 4 = 7$ bags. $7 \times 90\text{p} = 630\text{p} = £6.30$.

**Answer: (E) £6.30**

solutions.title: Total grams
solutions.body:
In 28 days he eats $28 \times 20 = 560$ g, which is $560 \div 80 = 7$ bags, costing £6.30.

**Answer: (E) £6.30**

prompt:
Pat and Sam like to sit at either end of their sofa, with their three children sitting between them.

In how many ways can they do this?

solutions.title: List the children
solutions.body:
Call the children A, B and C. Their orders in the middle are ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA: 6 ways. For each, Pat can be on the left and Sam on the right, or the other way round: $6 \times 2 = 12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

solutions.title: Seat by seat
solutions.body:
Left end: 2 choices (Pat or Sam); right end: the other parent. Middle seats: 3 choices, then 2, then 1. Total $2 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt:
Mr Waddle walks at 2 mph and Mr Ramble walks at 4 mph.

They set off together for a non-stop 12 mile hike.

How long after Mr Ramble finishes does Mr Waddle complete the hike?

solutions.title: Time for each
solutions.body:
Mr Waddle takes $12 \div 2 = 6$ hours and Mr Ramble $12 \div 4 = 3$ hours. The difference is 3 hours.

**Answer: (B) 3 hours**

solutions.title: Where is Mr Waddle?
solutions.body:
When Mr Ramble finishes after 3 hours, Mr Waddle has walked $3 \times 2 = 6$ miles and has 6 miles left, which takes him another 3 hours.

**Answer: (B) 3 hours**

prompt:
I add together three consecutive whole numbers.

Their sum is **always**

solutions.title: Balance around the middle
solutions.body:
The smallest number is 1 less than the middle one and the largest is 1 more. So the three add up to three times the middle number — always a multiple of 3.

**Answer: (E) a multiple of 3**

solutions.title: Try examples
solutions.body:
$1+2+3 = 6$ (even, not a multiple of 5), $2+3+4 = 9$ (odd, not prime), $4+5+6 = 15$. Only "a multiple of 3" is true every time.

**Answer: (E) a multiple of 3**

prompt:
Miss Fitt likes to line her class up in different ways.

When all the pupils are there she can line them up in twos, or in threes or in fives, with nobody left over.

What is the smallest number she could have in her class for that to be true?

solutions.title: Common multiple
solutions.body:
The number must be a multiple of 2, 3 and 5. The smallest is $2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30$.

**Answer: (C) 30**

solutions.title: Check the options
solutions.body:
15 and 45 are odd (not in twos); 20 is not a multiple of 3; 30 and 60 both work, and 30 is smaller.

**Answer: (C) 30**

prompt:
Five girls are sitting around a table.

Each girl makes a "high five" with each of the other girls.

How many "high fives" are made?

solutions.title: One girl at a time
solutions.body:
Ava high-fives the other 4. Bina still has 3 new girls, Clare 2 and Dora 1 (Elph). Total $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

solutions.title: Count and halve
solutions.body:
Each of the 5 girls makes 4 high fives: $5 \times 4 = 20$. But each high five involves two girls and was counted twice, so there are $20 \div 2 = 10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

prompt:
Isaac is 53 years old. His mother is 81.

How many years ago was Isaac's age one third of his mother's age then?

solutions.title: Use the age gap
solutions.body:
The age gap is always $81 - 53 = 28$ years. When his mother was three times his age, the gap was twice Isaac's age, so Isaac was $28 \div 2 = 14$ (and his mother 42). That was $53 - 14 = 39$ years ago.

**Answer: (E) 39**

solutions.title: Test the options
solutions.body:
39 years ago Isaac was $53 - 39 = 14$ and his mother $81 - 39 = 42$, and $14 = \frac{1}{3} \times 42$ ✓.

**Answer: (E) 39**

prompt:
The floor of Milo's rectangular bedroom is completely covered with square carpet tiles.

When he measures the room in tiles, he finds it is 11 tiles long and 8 tiles wide.

How many of the carpet tiles do **not** touch the walls?

solutions.title: Inner rectangle
solutions.body:
Remove the outer ring of tiles: the tiles left form a rectangle $(11 - 2)$ by $(8 - 2)$, that is $9 \times 6 = 54$ tiles.

**Answer: (D) 54**

solutions.title: Total minus edge tiles
solutions.body:
There are $11 \times 8 = 88$ tiles. Edge tiles: $2 \times 11 + 2 \times 8 - 4 = 34$ (the 4 corners were counted twice). $88 - 34 = 54$.

**Answer: (D) 54**

prompt:
Penny has one of each of the coins 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p and 50p. She places each of them inside the shapes on a diagram like the one shown here.

The money in the circle amounts to 61p and the money in the square amounts to 38p.

Which two coins go in the overlapping region?

solutions.title: Find what is counted twice
solutions.body:
All six coins add up to $1 + 2 + 5 + 10 + 20 + 50 = 88$p. The circle and square together give $61 + 38 = 99$p. The extra $99 - 88 = 11$p is the overlap, counted twice. The only two coins making 11p are 10p and 1p.

**Answer: (A) 10p and 1p**

solutions.title: Build it
solutions.body:
The circle needs 61p: $50 + 10 + 1$. The square needs 38p: $20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1$. The 10p and 1p are in both, so they go in the overlap, and every coin is used exactly once.

**Answer: (A) 10p and 1p**

prompt:
The large square shown is divided into smaller squares.

What fraction is shaded?

solutions.title: Add the pieces
solutions.body:
The large square is a 4 by 4 grid. The four shaded corner squares are each $\frac{1}{16}$, together $\frac{4}{16} = \frac14$. The middle 2 by 2 block is $\frac14$ of the square and is split into 9 tiny squares, 3 of them shaded: $\frac39 \times \frac14 = \frac{1}{12}$. Total $\frac14 + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{3}{12} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac13$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{1}{3}$**

solutions.title: Measure in tiny squares
solutions.body:
The middle 2 by 2 block of grid squares is made of 9 tiny squares, so one grid square is worth $\frac94$ tiny squares. The whole square (16 grid squares) is worth $16 \times \frac94 = 36$ tiny squares. Shaded: the 4 corners are worth $4 \times \frac94 = 9$, plus 3 tiny squares in the middle: 12 out of 36, which is $\frac13$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{1}{3}$**

prompt:
$JKLM$ is a square.

Another square $PQRS$ touches the midpoint of each of the sides of $JKLM$.

The perimeter of $JKLM$ is 48 cm.

What is the area of triangle $RMS$ in square centimetres?

solutions.title: Fraction of the square
solutions.body:
Each side of $JKLM$ is $48 \div 4 = 12$ cm. Joining the midpoints cuts off four equal corner triangles, which together make half the square, so each is $\frac18$ of it. The square's area is $12 \times 12 = 144$ cm², so triangle $RMS$ is $144 \div 8 = 18$ cm².

**Answer: 18**

solutions.title: Half base times height
solutions.body:
$R$ and $S$ are midpoints, so $MR = MS = 6$ cm and the angle at $M$ is a right angle. Area $= \frac12 \times 6 \times 6 = 18$ cm².

**Answer: 18**

prompt:
The diagram shows a square and a regular hexagon touching a straight line and overlapping.

What is the size of the angle marked $x°$?

solutions.title: Find the triangle under the overlap
solutions.body:
Let $Q$ be the square's corner on the line and $R$ the hexagon's corner on the line, and let $X$ be the point where the square's right edge crosses the hexagon's left edge (the angle $x°$ is at $X$, above the line).
- At $Q$: $180° - 21° - 90° = 69°$ between the line and the square's right edge.
- At $R$: each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, so $180° - 120° - 21° = 39°$ between the line and the hexagon's left edge.
- In triangle $QRX$ the angle at $X$ is $180° - 69° - 39° = 72°$.
- The angle $x°$ is on a straight line with it: $x = 180 - 72 = 108$.

**Answer: 108°**

solutions.title: Exterior angle
solutions.body:
Using the same triangle $QRX$: the angle $x°$ is the exterior angle at $X$, so it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: $69° + 39° = 108°$.

**Answer: 108°**

prompt:
More than 60% but less than 65% of the spiders in my cupboard have hairy legs.

What is the smallest number of spiders that could be in my cupboard?

solutions.title: Try each number of spiders
solutions.body:
We need a fraction with that many spiders strictly between 60% and 65%.
- 1 to 5 spiders: possible percentages include 50%, 66.7%, 75%, 60%, 80% — none strictly between 60% and 65%.
- 6: 50%, 66.7% — no. 7: 57%, 71% — no.
- 8: $\frac58 = 62.5\%$ ✓

**Answer: 8**

solutions.title: Think of the gap
solutions.body:
Between 60% and 65% there is a gap of only 5%. The fraction $\frac{k}{n}$ must satisfy $0.6n < k < 0.65n$. For $n = 8$: $4.8 < k < 5.2$, so $k = 5$ works. For each smaller $n$ the interval $(0.6n, 0.65n)$ contains no whole number (e.g. $n = 7$: $4.2$ to $4.55$).

**Answer: 8**

prompt:
Three cats, Flopsie, Lopsie and Topsie, were weighed in pairs.

The weights of each of the three pairs were 5 kg, 8 kg and 9 kg.

What was the weight of the heaviest cat?

solutions.title: Add all the pairs
solutions.body:
Each cat was weighed twice, so $5 + 8 + 9 = 22$ kg is twice the total of the three cats. The three cats weigh 11 kg. The heaviest cat is not in the lightest pair (5 kg), so it weighs $11 - 5 = 6$ kg.

**Answer: 6 kg**

solutions.title: Find each cat
solutions.body:
Total 11 kg. Taking away each pair gives the third cat: $11 - 5 = 6$, $11 - 8 = 3$, $11 - 9 = 2$. Check: $3 + 2 = 5$, $6 + 2 = 8$, $6 + 3 = 9$ ✓. Heaviest: 6 kg.

**Answer: 6 kg**

prompt:
Tabitha writes down a four-digit number $N$.

She then rubs out one of the digits and creates a new three-digit number, $M$, with the three digits that are left (in the same order as before).

The difference between $N$ and $M$ is 2021.

What is Tabitha's original number $N$?

solutions.title: Which digit was rubbed out?
solutions.body:
If she rubbed out any digit except the last, $N$ and $M$ would end in the same digit and $N - M$ would end in 0. But 2021 ends in 1, so she rubbed out the last digit $s$. Then $N = 10M + s$, so $N - M = 9M + s = 2021$. The largest multiple of 9 not more than 2021 is $2016 = 9 \times 224$, leaving $s = 5$. So $M = 224$ and $N = 2245$.

Check: $2245 - 224 = 2021$ ✓

**Answer: 2245**

solutions.title: Estimate, then check
solutions.body:
Taking the last digit off a four-digit number makes it about 10 times smaller, so $N - M$ is about $9M$. Then $M$ is about $2021 \div 9 \approx 224.6$. Try $M = 224$: we need $N = 224 + 2021 = 2245$, and rubbing out its last digit does give 224 ✓.

**Answer: 2245**
